amendments.why: The chapter fused an article into a single-word adverbial rendering six times — `הַיּוֹם` → *to day* (9.12 twice, 9.19), *now* (9.9), *ago* (9.20), `כַּיּוֹם` → *first* (9.27) and `הַחוּצָה` → *abroad* (9.26) — and split the same noun where the ASV wrote a determiner of its own (9.13 *at this time*). Rule 30's `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` sentence says a separately segmented article takes a written *the* or goes `unrepresented`, which read out of its context directs the opposite, and rule 32 lists `הַחוּצָה` → *out* without saying where the article goes. The corpus carries the chapter's reading rather than contradicting it: it aligns `הַיּוֹם` to *to day* as one Td+Ncmsa unit headed on *day* in ten units, and reads `כָּל־הַיָּמִים` → *for ever* as one Ncmsc+Td+Ncmpa unit in seven. The amendment adds that paragraph and the test that tells the two shapes apart, and changes nothing else in the rule.
amendments.rule: Where English fuses several morphemes into one word, such as *wherein*, they share a unit **only when that shared English rendering carries the sense of every morpheme placed in it**. Reserve `added` for English that no morpheme licenses at all. This governs a fixed multi-word Hebrew expression the ASV renders with one English word too, but it never absorbs a morpheme whose sense that rendering does not carry: in `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles*, the two lexical nouns may share *chronicles*, while the separately segmented article takes a written *the* or is its own `unrepresented` unit; `אִם לֹא` → *surely* may share one unit when *surely* carries both morphemes' senses. Such a fused expression is headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme, rather than leaving another morpheme whose sense the rendering carries `unrepresented`. The one-English-word condition is load-bearing in both directions: `בְּיַד` → *by* and `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* fuse, but where the ASV spends a second English word on the expression — `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses while the same idiom as *say ... nay* does not — the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. **Read that condition as one English rendering, not one English token.** A compound English preposition written in two or three words — *because of*, *by reason of*, *out of* — is a single rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and it fuses; so does an expression whose unit additionally carries a copula or other word the construction hands to the whole of it under another rule, as `לִפְנֵי` → *was before*. What defeats the condition is English the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so that each morpheme has a rendering of its own: `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives *to* to the preposition and *meet* to `פָּנֶה`, and `עַד לְ` → *until there was* gives *until* to `עַד` and the predicate's supplied copula to the `לְ` under rule 49, while the same `עַד לְ` → *to* fuses. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the second English word and ask whether a particular morpheme has lost its rendering or only the expression as a whole is diminished. What the second morpheme is tagged does not matter; a preposition before a construct noun fuses on the same terms as a compound preposition. **And such a compound's single English word carries the preposition's own relation even where no part of it states that relation separately.** Where `מִן`, `לְ`, `בְּ` or `עַל` stands before a construct noun and the ASV writes one English preposition for the pair, the condition is met and the two share a unit headed on the construct noun: `מִפְּנֵי` → *before*, `לִפְנֵי` → *before*, `עַל־פְּנֵי` → *upon*, `בְּקֶרֶב` → *among*. **Read that list as the commonest prepositions and not as a closed one:** what licenses the fusion is that a preposition stands on a construct noun and one English rendering carries the pair, so a `כְּ`, an `אֶל`, an `אַחַר` or any other preposition in that position is read on exactly the same terms, and `כְּפִי` → *as* fuses as `לְפִי` and `מִפְּנֵי` do. Do not read this rule's first sentence as requiring a separate English trace of the ablative, directional or locative sense before fusing, and do not mark the preposition `unrepresented` beside a construct noun holding the whole word: that is the outcome the fusion sentence above forbids and the one rule 22's closing paragraph forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a word, and the subtraction test finds no second English word for either morpheme to own. **The same prohibition runs the other way, and the construct noun is the side more often mistaken.** Do not mark the construct noun `unrepresented` beside a preposition holding the whole rendering either: the noun of such a compound is not a word the ASV ever writes alone, its sense is inside the one English word exactly as the preposition's is, and the reasoning that forbids the one direction forbids the other, so the two share a unit headed on the construct noun as before. Read whether any English word in the expression renders that noun's own lexeme, which is this rule's subtraction test again: `כְּפִיךָ` → *even as* ... *art* writes nothing for `פֶּה` in particular, so the pair fuses and the suffix keeps only the *thou* rule 18 writes for it, while `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives `פָּנֶה` a word of its own and rule 2 splits it. A pronominal suffix on the construct noun is no part of the fusion in either case: it takes whatever English pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18, or goes `unrepresented` under rule 40 where the ASV writes none, and its presence is not evidence that the preposition and its noun have separate renderings. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — `מִפְּנֵי` → *from before*, `מִקֶּרֶב` → *from among* — each morpheme has a rendering of its own, the condition is unmet, and rule 2 splits them; what tells the two shapes apart is independently recoverable ownership under rule 2, not the raw number of English words or which senses an English preposition leaves implicit. The corpus fuses `מִפְּנֵי` to *before* in fifteen units and to *because of* in seventy-five, `לִפְנֵי` to *before* in five hundred and ninety-seven, and a preposition with `תּוֹךְ` or `קֶרֶב` to *among* in twenty-seven. Contiguity is part of the condition for such an expression: a verb and the preposition it governs, held apart by the subject or the object, is not one. It is not a condition on fusion generally — rule 35's *Nor* and *never* fuse across intervening material, because there the one English word still carries every morpheme's sense. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* and `הוֹסִיף ... אֶל` → *exceed* are a verb whose preposition the ASV's comparative recasting leaves unrendered, so rule 2 splits them and the preposition is `unrepresented`. Rule 22 governs a repetition of the *same* element, not the parts of an idiom. **The expression need not be an idiom, and a full lexical noun fuses on the same terms as a function morpheme.** Where Hebrew writes a generic head noun before an attributive that names the class — `אִשָּׁה` or `אִישׁ` before a participle or an adjective — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme: `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* is one unit headed on `זוֹנָה`, with the indefinite article going to that nominal expression under rule 15, and `אִשָּׁה` is not marked `unrepresented` beside it. The one-English-word condition and its subtraction test decide this exactly as they decide a compound preposition — dropping the English word diminishes only the expression as a whole, and no morpheme owns a part of it — so where the ASV instead spends a word on each, as `אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה` → *man of war*, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. Do not read *fixed multi-word Hebrew expression* above as a requirement that the pair be idiomatic. **And a demonstrative modifying a noun is such an attributive.** Where Hebrew writes a noun with the demonstrative that modifies it — `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` and the like — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit on exactly the terms just given, headed on the morpheme whose lexeme that word most directly writes, which is ordinarily the demonstrative; an article standing in the phrase takes a written *the* under rule 29 or is its own `unrepresented` unit where the ASV writes none, exactly as the article of `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles* is. `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *thus* and `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *that* both fuse, and JDG.8.1 and JDG.8.3 are the two renderings in one chapter. **And a single English word that is one morpheme's own ordinary rendering does not defeat the condition.** What defeats it is a second English word the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so where one word alone stands for the whole expression the pair fuses even though that word is what the ASV writes for one of the morphemes elsewhere: this is rule 40's ruling that a preposition and its noun recast as one English adverb fuse though the word is the noun's ordinary rendering, and it is this rule's own `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's*, where *harlot's* is `זוֹנָה`'s own word and `אִשָּׁה` is still not marked `unrepresented`. Do not mark the other morpheme `unrepresented` on that ground, and do not reach for rule 22's first sentence, which governs an element the ASV has left unwritten and not one whose sense stands inside a fused word. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *this thing* — the condition is unmet, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. **And an article standing on the noun of such a fused expression shares the unit where the one English rendering carries its determination.** Where an article, the noun it determines, and a prefixed preposition or a directive `he` standing with them are rendered by a single English adverb — `הַיּוֹם` → *to day*, *now* or *ago*, `כַּיּוֹם` → *first*, `הַחוּצָה` → *abroad* — the English names the definite thing the article determines and no word is written for any one of those morphemes apart from the others, so all of them share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme, exactly as rule 40 fuses `בֶּאֱמֶת` → *faithfully* and rule 32 fuses a host with its directive `he`. Do not set the article outside such a unit on the strength of this rule's `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` sentence: what that sentence governs is an article determining the *nomen rectum* of a chain whose one English word writes the two nouns' lexemes and says nothing of their determination, and there the ASV's own *the* stands ready for the article whenever it is written. Test by the subtraction this rule already runs — drop the English word and ask whether the determination as well as the lexeme has gone unsaid. Where the ASV instead writes a determiner of its own for the article, the condition is unmet, rule 2 splits the expression, and each morpheme takes the word written for it: `כְּהַיּוֹם` → *at this time* gives *at* to the `כְּ`, *this* to the article under rule 41 and *time* to the noun, and one chapter may write both shapes, as 1SA.9.13 and 1SA.9.27 do. The corpus aligns `הַיּוֹם` to *to day* as one article-and-noun unit headed on *day* in ten units, and reads `כָּל־הַיָּמִים` → *for ever* as one unit with the article inside it in seven. **For this rule, a particle's single idiomatic English rendering includes the pronouns the English formula requires.** The entreaty particle `נָא` → *I beseech thee* or *we pray thee* takes the complete formula, headed on *beseech* or *pray*; its English subject and object pronouns are not `added`, because they realize the particle's one entreaty rather than supply arguments of the neighbouring imperative. Where the ASV's formula omits an object, as *I pray*, align only what it writes.

conventions: Temporal clauses in this chapter are asyndetic as often as not, and the subordinator is placed by the count rules 14 and 55 require. Where a fronted `הֵמָּה` opens the clause with no conjunction morpheme in it, the subordinator the ASV supplies is its own `added` unit — *When* (9.5), *As* (9.11, 9.27) — and where the ASV writes a coordinator beside it the two words stand together and are one `added` unit headed on the subordinator (9.14 *and as*). Where a waw does stand at the clause head it takes the whole pair as one rendering, headed on the coordinator (9.17, 9.25 *And when*).

Supplied English pronouns and nouns denoting a referent are placed by rule 25's condition read on the verse alone. Where the verse writes a nominal for the referent earlier than the clause in question, the further English realization joins that nominal's discontinuous unit: *he* of *he was higher* on `שָׁאוּל` (9.2), *he is a man* on `אִישׁ` (9.6), *it* of *hath it been kept* on `הַנִּשְׁאָר` (9.24), and both *is now called* and *was beforetime called* on the one `יִקָּרֵא` (9.9). Where the verse writes no such nominal, or writes it only in a later clause of its own, the supplied word is `added`: *they* of *there they were not* (9.4), the italic *he* of *he is before thee* (9.12), the italic *Samuel* (9.24). A supplied object pronoun with no object morpheme in the clause is `added` in either case (9.4 twice, 9.24 twice, rule 44).

`יֵשׁ` is read on the terms rule 50 sets for an interrogative existential clause. In `הֲיֵשׁ בָּזֶה הָרֹאֶה` → *Is the seer here* the one fronted *Is* is the interrogative particle's under rules 17 and 20 and the written `יֵשׁ` is `unrepresented`, nothing being left for it (9.11); where no interrogative particle stands, `יֵשׁ` takes the whole overt frame the ASV writes for it and heads on it — *He is* (9.12).

Read whether any English word in the expression renders that noun's own lexeme, which is this rule's subtraction test again: `כְּפִיךָ` → *even as* ... *art* writes nothing for `פֶּה` in particular, so the pair fuses and the suffix keeps only the *thou* rule 18 writes for it, while `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives `פָּנֶה` a word of its own and rule 2 splits it. A pronominal suffix on the construct noun is no part of the fusion in either case: it takes whatever English pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18, or goes `unrepresented` under rule 40 where the ASV writes none, and its presence is not evidence that the preposition and its noun have separate renderings. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — `מִפְּנֵי` → *from before*, `מִקֶּרֶב` → *from among* — each morpheme has a rendering of its own, the condition is unmet, and rule 2 splits them; what tells the two shapes apart is independently recoverable ownership under rule 2, not the raw number of English words or which senses an English preposition leaves implicit. The corpus fuses `מִפְּנֵי` to *before* in fifteen units and to *because of* in seventy-five, `לִפְנֵי` to *before* in five hundred and ninety-seven, and a preposition with `תּוֹךְ` or `קֶרֶב` to *among* in twenty-seven. Contiguity is part of the condition for such an expression: a verb and the preposition it governs, held apart by the subject or the object, is not one. It is not a condition on fusion generally — rule 35's *Nor* and *never* fuse across intervening material, because there the one English word still carries every morpheme's sense. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* and `הוֹסִיף ... אֶל` → *exceed* are a verb whose preposition the ASV's comparative recasting leaves unrendered, so rule 2 splits them and the preposition is `unrepresented`. Rule 22 governs a repetition of the *same* element, not the parts of an idiom. **The expression need not be an idiom, and a full lexical noun fuses on the same terms as a function morpheme.** Where Hebrew writes a generic head noun before an attributive that names the class — `אִשָּׁה` or `אִישׁ` before a participle or an adjective — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme: `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* is one unit headed on `זוֹנָה`, with the indefinite article going to that nominal expression under rule 15, and `אִשָּׁה` is not marked `unrepresented` beside it. The one-English-word condition and its subtraction test decide this exactly as they decide a compound preposition — dropping the English word diminishes only the expression as a whole, and no morpheme owns a part of it — so where the ASV instead spends a word on each, as `אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה` → *man of war*, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. Do not read *fixed multi-word Hebrew expression* above as a requirement that the pair be idiomatic. **And a demonstrative modifying a noun is such an attributive.** Where Hebrew writes a noun with the demonstrative that modifies it — `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` and the like — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit on exactly the terms just given, headed on the morpheme whose lexeme that word most directly writes, which is ordinarily the demonstrative; an article standing in the phrase takes a written *the* under rule 29 or is its own `unrepresented` unit where the ASV writes none, exactly as the article of `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles* is. `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *thus* and `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *that* both fuse, and JDG.8.1 and JDG.8.3 are the two renderings in one chapter. **And a single English word that is one morpheme's own ordinary rendering does not defeat the condition.** What defeats it is a second English word the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so where one word alone stands for the whole expression the pair fuses even though that word is what the ASV writes for one of the morphemes elsewhere: this is rule 40's ruling that a preposition and its noun recast as one English adverb fuse though the word is the noun's ordinary rendering, and it is this rule's own `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's*, where *harlot's* is `זוֹנָה`'s own word and `אִשָּׁה` is still not marked `unrepresented`. Do not mark the other morpheme `unrepresented` on that ground, and do not reach for rule 22's first sentence, which governs an element the ASV has left unwritten and not one whose sense stands inside a fused word. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *this thing* — the condition is unmet, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. **And an article standing on the noun of such a fused expression shares the unit where the one English rendering carries its determination.** Where an article, the noun it determines, and a prefixed preposition or a directive `he` standing with them are rendered by a single English adverb — `הַיּוֹם` → *to day*, *now* or *ago*, `כַּיּוֹם` → *first*, `הַחוּצָה` → *abroad* — the English names the definite thing the article determines and no word is written for any one of those morphemes apart from the others, so all of them share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme, exactly as rule 40 fuses `בֶּאֱמֶת` → *faithfully* and rule 32 fuses a host with its directive `he`. Do not set the article outside such a unit on the strength of this rule's `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` sentence: what that sentence governs is an article determining the *nomen rectum* of a chain whose one English word writes the two nouns' lexemes and says nothing of their determination, and there the ASV's own *the* stands ready for the article whenever it is written. Test by the subtraction this rule already runs — drop the English word and ask whether the determination as well as the lexeme has gone unsaid. Where the ASV instead writes a determiner of its own for the article, the condition is unmet, rule 2 splits the expression, and each morpheme takes the word written for it: `כְּהַיּוֹם` → *at this time* gives *at* to the `כְּ`, *this* to the article under rule 41 and *time* to the noun, and one chapter may write both shapes, as 1SA.9.13 and 1SA.9.27 do. The corpus aligns `הַיּוֹם` to *to day* as one article-and-noun unit headed on *day* in ten units, and reads `כָּל־הַיָּמִים` → *for ever* as one unit with the article inside it in seven. **For this rule, a particle's single idiomatic English rendering includes the pronouns the English formula requires.** The entreaty particle `נָא` → *I beseech thee* or *we pray thee* takes the complete formula, headed on *beseech* or *pray*; its English subject and object pronouns are not `added`, because they realize the particle's one entreaty rather than supply arguments of the neighbouring imperative. Where the ASV's formula omits an object, as *I pray*, align only what it writes.
amended.why: The chapter fused an article into a single-word adverbial rendering six times — `הַיּוֹם` → *to day* (9.12 twice, 9.19), *now* (9.9), *ago* (9.20), `כַּיּוֹם` → *first* (9.27) and `הַחוּצָה` → *abroad* (9.26) — and split the same noun where the ASV wrote a determiner of its own (9.13 *at this time*). Rule 30's `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` sentence says a separately segmented article takes a written *the* or goes `unrepresented`, which read out of its context directs the opposite, and rule 32 lists `הַחוּצָה` → *out* without saying where the article goes. The corpus carries the chapter's reading rather than contradicting it: it aligns `הַיּוֹם` to *to day* as one Td+Ncmsa unit headed on *day* in ten units, and reads `כָּל־הַיָּמִים` → *for ever* as one Ncmsc+Td+Ncmpa unit in seven. The amendment adds that paragraph and the test that tells the two shapes apart, and changes nothing else in the rule.

report: Checked all 67 candidate lemma groups and read the 27-verse dump end to end for the added-unit splits the table cannot see. No cross-verse split found; patches empty.

Asyndetic temporal clauses are consistent: a fronted `הֵמָּה` with a participle or perfect and no conjunction marks the supplied subordinator `added` in 9.5 (*When*), 9.11 and 9.27 (*As*), and the supplied coordinator-plus-subordinator pair as one `added` unit in 9.14 (*and as*); the two clauses that do write a waw, 9.17 and 9.25, give it *And when* whole under rule 55. The count is run on the Hebrew each time.

Other recurring constructions agree across their occurrences: `בָּמָה` → *high place* headed on *high* (9.12, 9.13, 9.14, 9.19, 9.25); the six `לִפְנֵי`/`לְפָנֶיךָ`/`לְפָנִים` fusions all headed on `פָּנֶה`; `בְּתוֹךְ` headed on the construct noun (9.14, 9.18); the supplied directional preposition on a directive `he` where one stands (9.13, 9.22) and on the bare noun under rule 33 where none does (9.14, 9.19, 9.25); rule 29's fronting case for an anarthrous rectum (9.7, 9.8, 9.10, 9.18) against its arthrous case (9.11, 9.26, 9.27) and its possessive case (9.3, 9.20).

The supplied-pronoun decisions divide on rule 25's own condition rather than arbitrarily: a further English realization joins the nominal the verse writes earlier (9.2 *he*, 9.6 *he is a man*, 9.9 both realizations of `יִקָּרֵא`, 9.24 *it*), and is `added` where the verse writes no such nominal or writes it only in a later clause of its own (9.4 *they*, 9.12 italic *he*, 9.24 italic *Samuel*). Recorded as a convention; the competing readings are already named in the unit notes.

BSB: 46 disagreements, all documented convention classes (R, C, Sh, Td, Rd) plus 9.11 `יֵשׁ`, 9.9 `וֹ` on the infinitive construct, the two paragogic nuns and the four object markers of 9.13 and 9.22. None is a genuine error: the interrogative clause follows rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential, and the 9.9 suffix follows rule 22 because the ASV writes the lexical noun as that clause's subject and no pronoun for the suffix. Nothing was changed to move the rate.

The three large-source units (9.6 *whereon*, 9.26 *abroad*, 9.27 *first*) are each a genuine fusion: rule 22's relative-preposition-suffix pronominal adverb, and two adverbial renderings of an article-and-noun with a directive `he` or a prefixed preposition.

One generalisation promoted, as an amendment to rule 30: an article standing on the noun of a fused expression shares the unit where the single English rendering carries its determination (`הַיּוֹם` → *to day*, *now*, *ago*; `כַּיּוֹם` → *first*; `הַחוּצָה` → *abroad*), and is split off only where the ASV writes a determiner of its own (9.13 *at this time*). Rule 30's `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` sentence reads out of context as directing the opposite; the corpus agrees with this chapter (ten `הַיּוֹם` → *to day* units headed on *day*, seven `כָּל־הַיָּמִים` → *for ever* with the article inside the unit).
